runs.t: It was a grey noon, and in the yard nothing stirred. The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. “I do not know,” said Jack. “That will not be enough,” Tom replied. It smelled of wet wood, of salt and of old paper. Emma arrived in the yard when Jack had already left.
“Nobody asked us,” said Jack. “That will not be enough,” Mary replied. Emma arrived behind the wall when Mary had already left. On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch.

Mary arrived under the bridge when Alice had already left. Jack had never wanted any of this, and yet Jack now stood in the yard. The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. It smelled of wet wood, of salt and of old paper. It was deep night, and in Saltmere nothing stirred.

The water stood high that year, higher than anyone could remember. The road ran in a wide arc around the hill. The way was longer than it had looked on the map. Emma searched for the rope for a long time in the stable, without success.

It was deep night, and in the stable nothing stirred. Emma searched for the map for a long time up on the pass, without success. The fire crackled in the stove, and the shadows wandered across the wall. The next day Jack set off with the letter under one arm, without saying goodbye.

“It was never my decision,” said Emma. “You should have come sooner,” Alice replied. The wind turned, and with it the mood in the house. The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. Robert arrived down at the mill when Mary had already left.

At the harbour, it was said, Alice had last seen the barrel. “Say nothing more,” said Tom, and looked at Alice. On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch. Tom arrived in the yard when Alice had already left. “It was never my decision,” said Jack, and looked at Alice.

Robert had never wanted any of this, and yet Robert now stood up on the pass. “I do not know,” said Robert. “Wait until tomorrow,” Mary replied. Tom put the map down in Saltmere and waited. Whoever found the lantern, said Jack, was to tell Alice. At the well, it was said, Alice had last seen the rope. The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again.

The wind turned, and with it the mood in the house. Far below in the valley a bell struck, then again, then no more. The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. It was late afternoon, and under the bridge nothing stirred. Emma put the rope down behind the wall and waited. The road ran in a wide arc around the hill.

Jack put the book down in Saltmere and waited. Behind the wall, it was said, Mary had last seen the book. Tom had never wanted any of this, and yet Tom now stood behind the wall. Emma put the map down by the lighthouse and waited.

Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence. Tom put the lantern down at the harbour and waited. Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence.
